extraction.name: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context
extraction.description: A large-scale dataset of complex everyday scenes containing common objects in their natural context, with per-instance segmentations for precise object localization.
extraction.creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The authors selected 91 object categories from multiple sources, then collected candidate images primarily by searching Flickr using object-object and object-scene keyword combinations to obtain non-iconic images; they also used explicit filtering to remove iconic images when needed.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Candidate images downloaded from Flickr photo metadata/search results, supplemented by images found via object-object and scene/object keyword searches; the dataset ultimately contains 328,000 images.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: An AMT filtering task was used to remove invalid or iconic images from candidate grids; for category labeling, workers dragged and dropped category icons onto corresponding object instances, with instructions designed to encourage annotating all categories present and only a single instance of each object category needed.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Annotation quality was analyzed by comparing crowd worker quality to dedicated expert workers using precision and recall; ground truth was computed using majority vote of the experts.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Dedicated expert workers were co-authors of the paper; crowd workers were AMT workers.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset is intentionally biased toward non-iconic, everyday scenes and entry-level 'thing' categories, and excludes 'stuff' categories; the authors also note that categories were selected to be balanced across super-categories and that images were collected to contain rich contextual relationships.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The paper notes that the dataset does not include 'stuff' categories, limits categories to entry-level labels, and may not cover categories that were difficult to collect at scale; it is designed for precise object-instance localization rather than all scene elements.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is presented as advancing computer vision and scene understanding, with potential benefits for practical applications through improved object recognition, localization, and contextual reasoning.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Intended for training and evaluating object recognition, object detection, and instance segmentation systems, especially for non-iconic views, contextual reasoning, and precise 2D localization; the paper also provides baseline performance analysis for bounding box and segmentation detection.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: To boost recall, the location of the instance found by a worker in the previous stage was shown to the current worker; workers could also use a magnifying glass to find small instances.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were collected from Flickr and scene/object pair searches, with an explicit filtering stage to remove iconic images; categories were selected and limited to 91 entry-level 'thing' categories, removing categories with fewer than 5,000 instances.

name.evidence: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context

description.evidence: We present a new dataset ... by gathering images of complex everyday scenes containing common objects in their natural context. Objects are labeled using per-instance segmentations to aid in precise object localization.

inLanguage.evidence: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context

rai:dataCollection.evidence: “We collected non-iconic images using two strategies. First ... we collected images from Flickr ... Second, we did not search for object categories in isolation... we searched for pairwise combinations of object categories... To further supplement our dataset we also searched for scene/object category pairs... In the rare cases in which enough images could not be found, we searched for single categories and performed an explicit ﬁltering stage to remove iconic images.”

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: “we collected images from Flickr” and “we searched for pairwise combinations of object categories”

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: “we collected images from Flickr which tends to have fewer iconic images... we searched for pairwise combinations of object categories... To further supplement our dataset we also searched for scene/object category pairs... The result is a collection of 328,000 images”

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: “we created an AMT ﬁltering task that allowed users to remove invalid or iconic images from a grid of 128 candidates” and “We designed the labeling task to encourage workers to annotate all categories present in the image. Workers annotate categories by dragging and dropping icons from the bottom category panel onto a corresponding object instance. Only a single instance of each object category needs to be annotated in the image.”

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: “we created an AMT ﬁltering task” and “the union of 8 AMT workers”

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: “We analyzed crowd worker quality on the category labeling task by comparing to dedicated expert workers” and “Ground truth was computed using majority vote of the experts.”

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: “the union of 8 AMT workers, the same number as was used to collect our labels”

rai:annotatorDemographics.evidence: “seven expert workers (co-authors of the paper)” and “the union of 8 AMT workers”

rai:dataBiases.evidence: “Our goal was to collect a dataset such that a majority of images are non-iconic” and “we decided to only include ‘thing’ categories and not ‘stuff.’”

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: “we decided to only include ‘thing’ categories and not ‘stuff.’” and “Categories for which obtaining a large number of instances (greater than 5,000) was difficult were also removed.”
